Independence movements are organized efforts by colonized or subordinated peoples to gain political sovereignty and end foreign domination. The most prominent was the Indian independence movement from 1857 to 1947, which mobilized millions against British colonial rule through nonviolent resistance and political organization, culminating in Indian independence and partition. The broader phenomenon of decolonization—the end of European colonial empires in Asia and Africa from 1945 to 1980—represented a fundamental geopolitical shift that reshaped the global order and inaugurated the postcolonial world.

The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, evolved from a debating society into a mass political movement challenging British rule. Early leaders petitioned for reforms within the empire. Mohandas Gandhi transformed the movement through satyagraha, nonviolent resistance, reframing independence as a moral imperative. His campaigns of civil disobedience—the salt march and boycotts—mobilized peasants and workers on an unprecedented scale.

World War II accelerated decolonization. Britain's military exhaustion and India's strategic importance in the Pacific War strengthened independence negotiators. The Quit India movement in 1942 forced Britain to commit to withdrawal. Partition in 1947 split British India into the independent nations of India and Pakistan, with communal violence claiming at least one million lives and displacing fifteen million people—a foundational trauma in South Asian history. India achieved independence under Jawaharlal Nehru as prime minister. Gandhi was assassinated by a Hindu nationalist in 1948, within months of independence.

The success of nonviolent resistance inspired decolonization movements worldwide. Gandhi's methods influenced civil rights activists from Martin Luther King Jr. to Nelson Mandela. Colonial independence movements in Asia—Indonesia, Vietnam, Burma—and Africa—Kenya, Algeria, Ghana—followed in the 1950s and 1960s, often violently. Cold War rivalry accelerated imperial withdrawal. Dozens of new nations emerged, the United Nations membership nearly tripled, and former colonies asserted sovereignty though often struggling with poverty, authoritarian governance, and neocolonial economic dependence.
